Slide 01 — Context

Photos from assembly, put to a second use

These four photos were taken during the original build of this Reachy Mini Lite — a normal step of putting the kit together, nothing more. They sat unused until, later, Mitra — the Sanskrit-speaking agent this robot runs — stopped hearing anything.

Every software-side check at that point came back clean: the daemon found the robot's own audio hardware correctly, macOS reported the device present, and its input-volume slider was already at maximum. Yet the live input meter, watched while speaking directly at the robot, never moved once — a combination that points away from software and toward the physical microphone. Pollen Robotics' own troubleshooting notes list exactly one likely cause: the microphone's flex cable, connected the wrong way round, or damaged.

That's when these assembly photos turned out to already show exactly the connector in question. What follows is a proper walkthrough of what they reveal — annotated as a teardown, doubling as a map for the live investigation.

Fig. 01Mainboard — side A

Slide 02 — The Mainboard, side A

Power in, signals out

This is the Reachy Mini Lite Board v1.0 — a printed circuit board (PCB): layers of copper traces etched onto a fibreglass substrate, carrying both power and data between components without a single loose wire. Its silkscreen credits three names — Seeed Studio (who manufacture it), Pollen Robotics (who designed the robot), and Hugging Face.

  • 1
    POWER_INWhere external power arrives. The motors draw far more current than a USB port alone can supply — this is why the robot needs its 7 V / 5 A wall adapter connected, not just a USB cable.
  • 2
    Coil + capacitorsThe copper-wound inductor and the two round capacitors beside it form a switching voltage regulator — it takes the incoming power and smooths it into the clean, steady voltages the rest of the board needs.
  • 3
    USB_IN / USB_OUT (ports H, K)
    A USB-C pass-through pair: the robot's own USB link comes in one port, and a second port carries a connection back out — letting a single cable double as a small hub.
  • 4
    Connectors E / F (GND · 6V8 · DATA)
    A 3-wire bus: one ground, one power, one shared data line. This is how the robot's motors are chained together instead of wiring each one back individually.
  • 5
    BUT_A / RST
    A general-purpose button and a hardware reset button, for recovering the board without unplugging anything.
Basics — what's that orange ribbon?

The wide orange strip running across the board is a flex cable (FPC/FFC): a flat, bendable ribbon that connects two circuit boards through tight or moving spaces, replacing a bundle of separate wires with one thin strip. We'll follow this exact cable to where it plugs in, two slides from now. Reference — flexible flat cable ↗

Fig. 02Mainboard — side B

Slide 03 — The Mainboard, side B

The same board, flipped over

Turning the board reveals the connector this whole search was for: a small header printed MIC, upper-left, beside a cluster of support chips. This is almost certainly the exact connector Pollen's own troubleshooting page names first when a robot reports no audio input — orientation matters here, and a cable seated backwards produces precisely the symptom we'd been chasing: everything detected correctly, nothing actually heard.

  • 6
    MIC header
    The microphone's flex-cable connector. Check first: cable orientation, then whether the flex itself is creased or torn.
  • 7
    22-pin daughterboard (GND · DP · DM · 5V)
    DP / DM are the standard names for USB's two data lines (Data+, Data−) — so this small board is very likely the chip that turns the camera and microphone signals into the separate USB devices a computer sees.
  • 3
    USB_IN / USB_OUT again
    Same pass-through pair as the other side, ports I and K here.
  • 5
    RST / BUT_A again
    The same reset and general-purpose button, visible from this angle.
◆ Where this connects back

This daughterboard is the literal hardware behind the CoreAudio device macOS reports as "Reachy Mini Audio" — the same device whose input-level meter, checked much later during live troubleshooting, sat at a flat, unmoving zero even with volume maxed. These assembly photos happen to be the only look anyone's had at this connector since.

Fig. 03Antenna bracket + driver board

Slide 04 — The Antennas

The "antennas" are motors, not aerials

Reachy Mini's two antennas don't receive radio signals — they're small expressive actuators, closer in spirit to ears that perk up than to anything on a walkie-talkie. The robot's own startup log confirms it plainly, configuring motors named right_antenna and left_antenna right alongside its head and body motors.

This bracket carries the mounting bearings for both antenna motors, with a small driver board screwed in between them — it converts commands arriving over the shared bus into small, precise movements, and reports position back the other way.

Basics — what's a "bus servo"?

An ordinary hobby servo gets its own dedicated wire back to a controller. A bus servo instead has an ID number and listens on a shared 3-wire line alongside every other motor — the same E/F connectors seen on the mainboard. That's how one small board can independently drive all eight of this robot's motors without eight separate cables. Reference — Dynamixel bus servos ↗

Fig. 04Head assembly, opened

Slide 05 — Inside the Head

A camera ribbon, and a memory card

The orange flex cable printed "Raspberry Pi Camera Cable" is a CSI-style ribbon connector — a standard first popularized by the Raspberry Pi Foundation for wiring a bare camera sensor straight to a board, since adopted widely enough that many non-Raspberry-Pi devices reuse the exact same connector. It runs from the camera sensor at the front of the head down to the mainboard.

The microSD card being handled here slots into the mainboard itself — standard practice on small embedded boards, typically holding local firmware or configuration rather than anything user-facing.

  • 8
    Camera cable
    Carries raw image data from the sensor up to the mainboard's interface chip — the same daughterboard from slide 03.
  • 9
    microSD card
    Local storage for the board's own firmware/configuration.

One honest limit of a photo like this: identifying the exact onboard chip with certainty isn't possible from the outside, so it's described here by what it does, not by name.

Fig. 04bFront sensor housing, lower half

Slide 06 — The Face

Two round ports, one small board

Lower in the same photo, the front shell holds two round housings on either side of a small green interface board — the same 22-pin connector style seen twice already. This is where the robot's face-forward sensors physically sit: Reachy Mini Lite's spec calls for a wide-angle camera and two microphones here, tucked directly behind where a face would be.

Which exact round housing is the camera lens and which is a microphone port isn't something a single photo can settle with certainty — reading a spec sheet is more reliable here than reading a photo.

Basics — why put sensors right up front?

For a desktop companion robot, the camera and microphones share the same job: paying attention to whoever's talking to it. Placing both together, aimed the same direction as the "face," keeps what it sees and what it hears pointed at the same person.
